edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE
edition.deck: A cockpit attack puts an Israel-bound flight in danger; diesel supplies, Ukraine’s bridges and major domestic disputes are also in focus.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and groups reports about the same event. Allegations, unresolved investigations and differing figures are attributed rather than presented as settled fact.

content.headline: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with crash axe, UAE says
content.shortHeadline: UAE says co-pilot attacked captain with crash axe
content.standfirst: Passengers helped subdue the co-pilot after the Israel-bound flight plunged sharply; reserve pilots landed it safely in Saudi Arabia. Investigators have not established the suspect’s motive.

image.caption: Captain Smit Machchhar, praised by India’s government for his courage during the attack.

sources.originalTitle: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE

segments.body: The UAE prosecutor general says the co-pilot of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv attacked the captain with a crash axe and tried to take control. The aircraft plunged about 17,000ft before passengers intervened. The Guardian reports 182 people were aboard; the BBC says more than 170.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The injured captain, Smit Machchhar, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the co-pilot. Two reserve pilots then diverted the plane and landed in Saudi Arabia. The UAE is leading an investigation, with other countries taking part.

Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has described the suspect as having undergone Islamist radicalisation. That claim has not established a motive: investigators say they are still working to determine what happened and whether anyone else was involved. Reports naming the suspect have not been officially confirmed.

content.headline: Russian strike damages a second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
content.shortHeadline: Russian strike damages second major Kyiv bridge
content.standfirst: The Northern Bridge was hit days after repeated attacks on the Southern Bridge, disrupting a key route across the capital. Ukraine says Moscow is targeting civilian infrastructure; Russia says the bridge serves military logistics.

image.caption: The Northern Bridge in Kyiv, the second major bridge reported hit in recent days.

sources.originalTitle: Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, mayor says
Russiske droneangreb skaber frygt i Kyiv: Borgere overvejer at forlade byen

segments.body: Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko says a Russian strike damaged the road surface and trolleybus wires on the Northern Bridge on Saturday, blocking traffic across the Dnipro. Russia’s defence ministry acknowledged striking the bridge, saying it was used for troop transfers and logistics.

segments.title: Disruption and wider attacks
segments.body: The strike followed repeated attacks on the Southern Bridge, which have suspended metro and car travel across it. The two bridges connect the eastern and western parts of the city. Ukrainian reporting describes residents’ fears as attacks continue, with some considering leaving Kyiv ahead of a difficult winter.

content.headline: Spain’s government loses housing vote after 87-year-old’s eviction
content.shortHeadline: Sánchez loses housing vote after eviction sparks protests
content.standfirst: Parliament rejected two tenant-protection decrees, deepening pressure on Pedro Sánchez’s minority government. The defeat follows protests over an older woman’s eviction and leaves the measures’ future uncertain.

image.caption: Pedro Sánchez made a last-minute appeal to allies to support the housing measures.

sources.originalTitle: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87

segments.body: Spain’s Congress rejected two government decrees intended to address the housing crisis, including measures to suspend some evictions and extend certain rental contracts. The votes were 178 to 172 and 184 to 166, leaving the proposals without parliamentary approval.

segments.title: Political pressure
segments.body: The measures followed protests triggered by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal after a sharp rent increase. Her landlord later negotiated her return at a lower rent, but demonstrations have continued. The defeat highlights Sánchez’s lack of a congressional majority and fuels speculation about an early election; no decision has been announced.

content.headline: French education protests disrupt hundreds of schools as clashes spread
content.shortHeadline: French school protests spread as police clash with students
content.standfirst: Demonstrations over staffing, overcrowding and run-down buildings have led to arrests, injuries and school closures. Authorities say the unrest is being joined by people who are not students.

image.caption: A fire burns in the street during a student blockade in Brest.

sources.originalTitle: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
Skoleelever over hele Frankrig demonstrerer

segments.body: Protests over conditions in French schools have spread beyond Paris, with disruption reported at hundreds of schools. The BBC reports 735 schools affected and 1,747 arrests; a separate TV 2 report gives different figures, citing more than 600 arrests and about 560 schools disrupted. The precise totals vary between reports.

segments.title: Grievances and violence
segments.body: Students cite a lack of replacement teachers, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities. The unrest has included fires and clashes with police; at least 65 education staff were reported injured by the French education ministry. A 17-year-old was arrested after an officer was attacked in Belfort, where video footage shows the officer being beaten.

content.headline: Bangkok floods kill about 40 as record rain overwhelms the city
content.shortHeadline: Bangkok floods kill 40 as heavy rain overwhelms drainage
content.standfirst: Floodwater turned neighbourhoods into lakes after roughly 300mm of rain fell in about two days. The disaster has disrupted travel and forced thousands into shelters, while scientists warn extreme rainfall risks are growing.

sources.originalTitle: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes

segments.body: About 40 people died in flood-related incidents in Bangkok, and thousands sought shelter, according to the Thai government. Some districts received roughly 300mm of rain in about two days. Floodwater covered streets and homes, disrupted the airport and closed schools.

segments.title: A city under strain
segments.body: Bangkok’s canals, pumps and dikes could not cope with the prolonged downpour. Residents described warnings arriving too late as water rose, and said debris and rubbish were left behind as levels began to fall. Authorities warned more heavy rain could come, while drainage could take days.

segments.title: Climate context
segments.body: Scientists say extreme rainfall is worsening in parts of south-east Asia and is expected to intensify as the planet warms. They have not attributed this particular flood to climate change: the rain was linked to a low-pressure system, and the influence of a strong El Niño pattern also complicates the picture.

content.headline: Brazil election pits Lula against Bolsonaro’s son in close race
content.shortHeadline: Brazil vote tests Lula and the rise of a pro-Trump bloc
content.standfirst: The close presidential contest is being watched as a test of regional politics and Donald Trump’s influence. The result remains uncertain, with a runoff possible if neither leading candidate wins a majority.

image.caption: Supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro at a rally in São Paulo.

sources.originalTitle: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
The knife-edge election Trump is watching as a blueprint for the midterms

segments.body: Brazilian voters are choosing between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Polls cited by the Guardian show a close race. If neither candidate wins more than half the vote, a runoff is scheduled for 25 October.

segments.title: Regional stakes
segments.body: The contest has become a test of a rightward shift across Latin America and of the region’s relationship with Washington. Lula has criticised Trump’s regional agenda; Bolsonaro has signalled alignment with it. Analysts cited in the reports say a Bolsonaro victory could strengthen the pro-Trump bloc, though the outcome and its implications remain uncertain.

segments.title: A divided campaign
segments.body: The candidates differ sharply over US influence, crime and Brazil’s natural resources. Lula’s campaign faces corruption allegations that are still under investigation; Bolsonaro is running while his father is under house arrest following a conviction for attempting to overturn the 2022 election result. Voters’ motivations include both support for Bolsonaro and opposition to Lula.

content.headline: Cornell rape allegations prompt renewed inquiry and legal reform pledge
content.shortHeadline: Cornell case reopens debate over rape allegations and consent
content.standfirst: A civil lawsuit has renewed scrutiny of a 2024 alleged assault at Cornell, while New York’s governor says she will seek to change a law concerning intoxication and consent. The men named in the suit deny the allegations.

image.caption: Cornell University in Ithaca, New York.

sources.originalTitle: Cornell frat house rape accuser 'under siege' online, says lawyer
‘They tried to bury it’: The frat house gang-rape case tearing America apart
Guvernør vil lukke smuthul efter omdiskuteret voldtægtssag

segments.body: A woman identified in court documents as Jane Doe alleges she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a Cornell fraternity house in 2024. The men deny the claims and have not faced criminal charges. The case returned to public attention after Doe filed a civil lawsuit; New York prosecutors have reopened a criminal inquiry.

segments.title: Dispute over the investigation
segments.body: The county prosecutor has said Doe’s original 2024 statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped. A transcript reported by CBS and cited by the i Paper records her saying she was incapacitated and had been raped. New York governor Kathy Hochul appointed state attorney general Letitia James to take over the investigation.

segments.title: Privacy and legal change
segments.body: Hochul says she wants to close a legal loophole that can make rape prosecutions more difficult when an alleged victim voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. Doe’s lawyer also says online users are trying to identify her; the reporting describes mistaken identifications and harassment. The allegations and any criminal responsibility remain unresolved.

content.headline: Christa Pike remains critically ill after failed Tennessee execution
content.shortHeadline: Pike critically ill after botched lethal-injection attempt
content.standfirst: Her lawyers say she is unconscious and on a ventilator after two doses of pentobarbital failed to kill her. Tennessee has halted executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review.

image.caption: Tennessee corrections commissioner Frank Strada in Nashville.

sources.originalTitle: US murderer Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after failed execution, lawyers say
Prison chief in Christa Pike case oversaw five ‘botched’ executions, lawyers say
Kvinde i respirator efter mislykket henrettelse
Dødsdømt kvinde overlevede indsprøjtning, men hvordan kunne det ske?

segments.body: Christa Pike, a 50-year-old Tennessee death-row prisoner, remained critically ill in hospital after a lethal injection failed on Wednesday. Her lawyers say she was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator. They have asked the court to preserve all evidence relating to the execution attempt.

segments.title: Questions over the procedure
segments.body: Pike’s lawyers allege that execution staff struggled to place intravenous lines and did not realise that veins had ruptured or that the drug may have entered tissue rather than her bloodstream. The state has defended its protocol; authorities have not explained what went wrong or said whether another attempt will be made.

segments.title: Wider scrutiny
segments.body: Governor Bill Lee suspended executions in Tennessee until the end of the year and ordered an independent review. The Guardian reports that lawyers have questioned the record of prison commissioner Frank Strada, citing other disputed executions under his leadership in Arizona and Tennessee. The state’s procedures and the review’s findings remain matters of scrutiny.

content.headline: G7 agrees 100m-barrel release as diesel prices hit record UK levels
content.shortHeadline: G7 to release oil and diesel as UK pump prices soar
content.standfirst: The coordinated move is intended to ease supply fears and avert a US export ban. UK haulage groups warn that record diesel costs could feed through to food prices and threaten transport businesses.

image.caption: Fuel prices at a petrol station in Bristol.

sources.originalTitle: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
Petulant Trump will feel empowered by world’s latest surrender to his demands
Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high

segments.body: G7 leaders agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves over four months, including a substantial diesel release within 20 days. US President Donald Trump dropped his threat to restrict US diesel exports. It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks or how quickly.

segments.title: UK cost pressures
segments.body: The RAC said the average UK diesel price reached 200.01p a litre, a record, on Friday. The Road Haulage Association says hauliers are paying about £350 more each week to fill an HGV than in February and warns that extra costs could raise food prices or force firms to close. It is urging ministers to pause planned fuel-duty increases and offer a rebate to essential users.

segments.title: A short-term buffer
segments.body: An energy expert cited by the i Paper says releasing reserves may ease immediate pressure and give businesses time to adapt, but it reduces the buffer available for future disruption until stocks are replenished. The measures do not resolve wider concerns about refining capacity or reliance on international supplies.

content.headline: RAF Fairford arrests: sixth suspect released on bail as inquiry continues
content.shortHeadline: Fairford suspect released on bail as police inquiry continues
content.standfirst: A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national was arrested over suspected preparation of terrorist acts linked to an incident near the Gloucestershire airbase. Five other men arrested earlier were also released on bail.

image.caption: A view of RAF Fairford, where an investigation followed reports of suspicious vehicles.

sources.originalTitle: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail

segments.body: A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national arrested in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts connected with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail. Police say searches of two properties in the area have ended and the investigation is continuing.

segments.title: Earlier arrests
segments.body: Five other men in their twenties, all UK nationals from London, were arrested after suspicious vehicles were reported near the airbase and later released on bail. Police have not set out evidence linking the incident to Iran. Iran has denied involvement; earlier claims by UK and US officials did not provide further details.

content.headline: Two men charged over alleged plot targeting Manchester Jewish community
content.shortHeadline: Two men charged over alleged Manchester terror plot
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege the men carried out reconnaissance at Jewish sites, including the Heaton Park synagogue, and obtained instructions to make a chlorine bomb. Both have been remanded in custody; the allegations have not been tested at trial.

image.caption: Police arrested the suspects in Manchester on 20 September.

sources.originalTitle: Men in court over alleged plot to target Manchester Jewish community

segments.body: Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, have appeared in court charged with preparing to commit or assist an act of terrorism. Prosecutors allege they researched potential targets in Manchester, including the Heaton Park synagogue and the city’s Jewish Museum, and sought instructions to make an explosive device.

segments.title: Case before the courts
segments.body: The men were arrested in Manchester on the eve of Yom Kippur and remanded in custody until their next hearing at the Old Bailey. The charge relates to alleged activity on or before 20 September. The prosecution says they were directed by another Iranian individual believed to be in Iran; that allegation has not been established in court.

content.headline: Poll finds 49% back UK rejoining EU, but Labour figures urge caution
content.shortHeadline: Poll finds more voters back rejoining the EU than oppose it
content.standfirst: A survey of 11,461 people found 49% support for rejoining and 28.5% opposition. Labour figures remain divided over whether reopening Brexit could grow the party’s vote or revive political divisions.

image.caption: A pro-EU campaigner calls for the UK to rejoin the bloc in Parliament Square.

sources.originalTitle: Half of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll finds

segments.body: A Messina Group poll commissioned by the Guardian found 49% of respondents backed the UK rejoining the EU, against 28.5% who opposed it. The survey questioned 11,461 people between 12 and 24 September and tested seven possible relationships with the bloc.

segments.title: Political choices
segments.body: The poll also found support for closer trade arrangements and a customs union. Almost a third said rejoining would require an in-out referendum; others thought a general election mandate or a parliamentary decision would be enough. The findings do not settle which approach voters would ultimately accept.

segments.title: Caution within Labour
segments.body: The Guardian reports that some Labour figures see closer EU ties as a potential boost to the party, while others fear reigniting Brexit divisions or strengthening Reform. Ministers cited in the report disagree about how far the UK should go; the government has not committed to rejoining.

content.headline: Hammersmith and Fulham warns council tax could rise by 150%
content.shortHeadline: London council warns it may need a 150% tax rise
content.standfirst: The borough says a sharp cut in central government funding could leave it needing a major increase to balance its budget. A Band D household could pay £29.11 more a week under the highest scenario.

image.caption: Angela Rayner introduced the funding rules that local authorities say will affect their grants.

sources.originalTitle: London Labour council warns it may raise council tax by 150%

segments.body: Hammersmith and Fulham council says it may need to increase its own council tax charge by as much as 150% in 2027–28 to balance its budget under current assumptions. The council estimates the increase would add £29.11 a week for a Band D household.

segments.title: Funding dispute
segments.body: The council says its government funding will fall from £150.5m in 2025–26 to £72.4m over the next four years under the new funding formula. Ministers say the formula redirects money towards areas with greater need and that councils decide their own tax levels. The borough argues deprivation measures do not reflect its needs.

content.headline: Nuclear chiefs consider cutting armed escorts for some waste shipments
content.shortHeadline: Plan could reduce armed guards on nuclear waste shipments
content.standfirst: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority says tailoring security to each shipment could save money without reducing safety. Critics and the Civil Nuclear Constabulary warn that any change must preserve protection amid heightened concern about hostile-state activity.

image.caption: A specialist train is used to transport nuclear material around the UK.

sources.originalTitle: Nuclear waste armed guards face cuts under cost-saving plan

segments.body: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority is proposing changes that could remove mandatory armed escorts for some shipments of nuclear material, including plutonium and enriched uranium. It says security should be matched to the risk of each journey and estimates some transport costs could fall by 10–20%.

segments.title: Security concerns
segments.body: A former Civil Nuclear Constabulary officer argues that dangerous material in transit needs a strong deterrent. A security expert cited by the i Paper says reducing escorts does not necessarily increase risk, but stresses that the public needs clear information about which loads would be affected.

perspectives.body: The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority says any changes would be agreed with government and regulators and would maintain safety and security. The Civil Nuclear Constabulary says the consequences of failure are too serious for protection to be compromised.

content.headline: Labour faces resistance over proposed welfare and pension changes
content.shortHeadline: Labour MPs warn over welfare and pension reform plans
content.standfirst: Reviews of disability benefits and youth unemployment are nearing publication as ministers consider changes, including voluntary alternatives to some cash payments. Rebel MPs say they will scrutinise the details.

image.caption: Imali Chislett, a Southampton claimant who says PIP helps meet her disability-related costs.

sources.originalTitle: The Labour mutiny Burnham faces over triple lock and welfare reforms
I’m a PIP claimant – here’s how I spend my £780 payment

segments.body: The government is awaiting reviews of Personal Independence Payment and young people not in employment, education or training as it considers welfare changes. The i Paper reports that one option under discussion is allowing some claimants to choose services or equipment instead of part of a cash payment; the proposal is described as voluntary.

segments.title: Claimants’ concerns
segments.body: Imali Chislett, who receives PIP, says cash gives her flexibility to meet disability-related costs, including transport, energy and wheelchair expenses. Disability organisations cited by the i Paper warn that reducing cash could harm wellbeing and increase poverty. Ministers have said no claimant would be forced to accept services or equipment instead.

segments.title: Political test
segments.body: Labour MPs who opposed earlier welfare changes say they will judge any proposals on the detail, including whether people are supported into work before benefits are reduced. Ministers are also considering sanctions for some young people who refuse employment support. The reviews and the government’s final plans are not yet published.

content.headline: Denmark’s citizenship pause leaves applicants uncertain about their future
content.shortHeadline: Citizenship freeze leaves thousands waiting in Denmark
content.standfirst: Applications are on hold while a committee considers screening applicants for anti-democratic views. A human-rights researcher questions whether the pause is compatible with Denmark’s obligations; affected families say the uncertainty may drive them to leave.

image.caption: Saeid Ashian and his wife, Mia; Ashian had been listed for citizenship before the process was paused.

sources.originalTitle: Saeid var næsten dansk statsborger. Nu er familien så utryg, at de overvejer at forlade Danmark
Eksperter: Danmark bryder konventioner, hvis 231 bestemte børn ikke får statsborgerskab

segments.body: Denmark has paused the processing of citizenship cases while a committee considers whether applicants can be screened for anti-democratic views. DR reports that 2,055 people were listed for parliamentary approval in January before the bill fell, leaving their cases on hold.

segments.title: Rights concerns
segments.body: Human-rights researcher Eva Ersbøll says applicants need clear, usable rules and argues that the pause may conflict with Denmark’s obligations under the citizenship convention. DR separately reports that 72 stateless children born in Denmark met the requirements in January, and says as many as 231 children could be affected. The legal assessment depends in part on how long cases remain suspended.

segments.title: A family left waiting
segments.body: Saeid Ashian, an Iranian-born engineer who works in Denmark, says he met the requirements and was listed for citizenship approval. His family say they want to stay, but the uncertainty over their status and their children’s future has made them consider leaving.

content.headline: Three teenagers charged over alleged shooting at family home in Kastrup
content.shortHeadline: Teens charged over 15 shots fired at Kastrup family home
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege the young men were paid to target a family with three children; nobody was injured. Two defendants also face allegations linked to other attempted killings and a fire.

image.caption: The Kastrup apartment building where shots were fired; no one inside was hit.

sources.originalTitle: Teenagere tiltalt for drabsforsøg efter skud mod lejlighed i Kastrup
Teenagere forsøgte at slå familie med tre børn ihjel i Kastrup, lyder anklage

segments.body: Three young men, who were 17, 17 and 18 at the time, have been charged with attempted murder over a shooting at a family’s flat in Kastrup in March. Prosecutors allege 15 shots were fired through the windows while the family, including three children, was inside. No one was hit.

segments.title: Alleged contract violence
segments.body: The prosecution says the teenagers were hired to carry out the attack. The detailed indictment, reported by TV 2, also alleges that two of the defendants were involved in other attempted killings and a fire in the days beforehand. All three deny the charges, according to DR; the case is due to begin in Copenhagen next year.

content.headline: Aarhus police investigate whether two attacks on women are connected
content.shortHeadline: Aarhus police probe possible link between two attacks
content.standfirst: Two women were attacked near Riis Skov months apart, leaving residents fearful of running alone after dark. Police say it is too early to confirm a connection and warn residents not to form private patrols.

image.caption: The area where police are investigating two attacks on women near Aarhus.

sources.originalTitle: Politiet efterforsker, om overfald på unge kvinder ved Risskov kan hænge sammen
Kvinder frygter løbetur efter flere episoder: - Det er virkelig uhyggeligt
Overfald på kvindelige løbere får Jacob til at samle bekymrede naboer til aftenture i skoven

segments.body: East Jutland Police are investigating whether two attacks on young women in the Risskov area of Aarhus are connected. One woman was attacked in July; another was knocked down and held down in late September. Police say it is too early to say whether the same person was responsible.

segments.title: Residents’ response
segments.body: Women who spoke to TV 2 say the incidents have made them change when and where they run, or avoid going out alone after dark. Some local fathers have proposed walking in small groups. Police advise residents not to create anything resembling a private security patrol, saying trained officers are responsible for safety.

segments.title: Police appeal
segments.body: Police say they will increase patrols in the area and are seeking witnesses to both attacks. They advise anyone who feels unsafe walking alone to arrange to go with others and to contact police with information.

content.headline: Greenland’s Kujalleq municipality halts alcohol sales and serving
content.shortHeadline: Alcohol sales suspended in southern Greenland municipality
content.standfirst: Naalakkersuisut imposed a temporary ban at Kujalleq’s request, citing children’s welfare and public safety. Officials have not said how long it will remain in force or detailed the incidents behind the decision.

image.caption: Narsaq, a town in Kujalleq municipality in southern Greenland.

sources.originalTitle: Grønlandsk kommune stopper salg af alkohol
Alkohol forbydes i grønlandsk kommune for befolkningens sikkerhed

segments.body: Greenland’s government, Naalakkersuisut, has temporarily banned the sale and serving of alcohol in Kujalleq, in the south of the country. The measure took effect on Friday after a request from the municipal council and will remain in place until the order is lifted.

segments.title: Safety concerns
segments.body: The government says the purpose is to protect children and public safety. The municipality’s mayor has cited serious consequences linked to alcohol, but the authorities have not specified which incidents prompted the request. The ban’s duration is unclear.

content.headline: Aalborg approves recovery plan for criticised care home
content.shortHeadline: Aalborg launches plan after care-home hygiene and medicine failings
content.standfirst: Fremtidens Plejehjem has faced criticism over hygiene and medication handling. The municipality’s plan adds management support, staff training and routines for sharing residents’ care information.

image.caption: Fremtidens Plejehjem in Nørresundby, where the municipality has approved a recovery plan.

sources.originalTitle: Kommune kaster redningskrans ud til ældre og ansatte på kritiseret plejehjem

segments.body: Aalborg Municipality has approved an action plan for Fremtidens Plejehjem in Nørresundby after criticism and several orders concerning hygiene and medication handling. The municipality says the problems have lasted a long time and have been difficult to resolve.

segments.title: Changes and oversight
segments.body: The plan includes regular handover meetings, training in the digital system used to document care and medication, an additional deputy manager and a new management model. The municipality’s senior-care committee says it will monitor whether the measures improve conditions for residents and staff.

content.headline: Student with chronic illness waits 13 months for disability grant decision
content.shortHeadline: Student waits 13 months for disability study support
content.standfirst: A 15-month average wait for some applications is raising concerns that disabled students may struggle to stay in education. The government says it will discuss ways to shorten delays.

sources.originalTitle: Hun kæmper med "usexede symptomer" og er strandet på lang venteliste

segments.body: Josefine Agnete Andersen, a student with ulcerative colitis, has waited 13 months for a decision on her application for a disability supplement to her student grant. She says her regular grant largely goes on rent, food and travel, and that her condition and fatigue make taking a job difficult.

segments.title: Longer waits
segments.body: TV 2 Nord reports that the average processing time can reach 15 months for some higher-education applicants when more medical documentation is needed. Applications rose substantially between 2016 and 2024; a 2025 change to documentation requirements has not reduced the wait so far.

The Association of Young People with Disabilities warns that long delays can create financial stress and contribute to students leaving education. Moderates’ policy spokesperson says he will discuss options for reducing the wait with the minister. If awarded, the supplement is paid retroactively, but Andersen says she needs help while she is studying.

content.headline: Study finds Danish cross-border shopping costs state less than estimated
content.shortHeadline: Research challenges estimate of tax lost to border shopping
content.standfirst: Researchers say the state lost about 415 million kroner in 2019 on selected goods, rather than the 1.16 billion estimated by the Tax Ministry. Their findings draw on shopping patterns during pandemic border closures.

image.caption: The German border was closed during the pandemic, preventing Danes from shopping across it.

sources.originalTitle: Staten taber ikke så mange penge på grænsehandel, som vi hidtil har troet, viser ny forskning
Studie af danskeres indkøbsvaner tegner nyt billede af grænsehandel

segments.body: A University of Copenhagen study estimates that cross-border shopping for goods such as sweets, crisps, beer and soft drinks cost the state 415 million kroner in 2019, excluding tobacco. The Tax Ministry’s estimate for the same category was 1.16 billion kroner.

segments.title: Different assumptions
segments.body: The researchers examined Danish purchases during the pandemic, when borders were closed, to see how much spending moved back to domestic shops. They say the ministry’s estimate assumes all money spent on these goods in Germany would otherwise have been spent in Denmark; their findings suggest that does not happen one-for-one.

segments.title: Implications for taxes
segments.body: The study found a stronger rise in domestic purchases among people living near the German border, with little measurable change among those living 120 kilometres or more away. The researchers say border shopping may therefore be less of a constraint on taxes for most households. The Tax Ministry told DR it had not had time to review the study.

content.headline: North Zealand coastal protection plan divides residents and municipalities
content.shortHeadline: Coastal plan divides residents over sand, stones and erosion
content.standfirst: Three municipalities plan to move 241,000 cubic metres of gravel and stone to protect the North Zealand coast. Some local groups fear harm to beaches and biodiversity; supporters say action is needed against stronger storms and rising seas.

sources.originalTitle: Frustration i Nordsjælland – frygter, at attraktive sandstrande ødelægges for altid

segments.body: Halsnæs, Helsingør and Gribskov want to move 241,000 cubic metres of gravel and stone from the seabed south-east of Samsø to North Zealand as part of the Nordkystens Fremtid coastal protection project. The plan is intended to reduce erosion and protect properties from severe storms.

segments.title: Concerns over impact
segments.body: Some coastal and dike associations fear the material could replace fine sand with stones, damage the beaches’ recreational value and harm marine biodiversity at the extraction site. They say some existing local defences work and question whether the project would benefit their stretches of coast.

segments.title: Support for action
segments.body: The municipalities say the project has been developed over many years with guidance from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency. Some local groups support proceeding, warning that stronger storms and rising sea levels make delay risky. The project’s cost is shared among affected property owners, municipalities and the state.

content.headline: Liz Harris on Grouper, streaming fraud and the restorative pull of Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris on streaming scams and the joy of making music together
content.standfirst: A viral second life for Grouper’s “Poison Tree” exposed how easily royalties can be stolen. For Harris, reforming her dream-pop trio Helen has offered a counterweight to an industry she has good reason to distrust.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has spent much of her career keeping the music industry at a distance. Then “Poison Tree”, a song she released in 2008, found a huge audience on TikTok—and someone else had fraudulently uploaded and registered it, collecting roughly six figures in earnings before Harris and her label reclaimed what was owed.

segments.title: A different kind of company
segments.body: Harris describes the viral discovery as a warning about platforms that many artists assume are more regulated than they are. Fake remixes and tracks with matching titles can mean a tedious cycle of chasing down infringements. “It’s rational that I have a fear of immersing myself more into the music industry,” she says.

Making Linda’s Head, the second album by Helen, has offered a more restorative experience. Against the solitary sound of Grouper, the trio lets Harris show a brighter, more social side of herself. She says practising with friends lifted her spirits while she was navigating medical difficulties.

content.headline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke: friendship through grief and change
content.shortHeadline: Erasure’s bond endures as Vince Clarke steps back from touring
content.standfirst: As Erasure prepare their 20th album, Andy Bell and Vince Clarke reflect on four decades of creative partnership and mutual support. Clarke will direct the tour remotely after the death of his wife, Tracy.

image.caption: Vince Clarke and Andy Bell of Erasure.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.body: Erasure’s long-running partnership has been tested by bereavement. Clarke’s wife, Tracy Hurley Martin, died of stomach cancer in 2024; Bell, who lost his partner Paul Hickey in 2012, became a source of support. Clarke says Bell gave him “all the love and support I could possibly ever want.”

segments.title: A changed tour
segments.body: The band’s new album, Radio!! Radio!!, will accompany a UK and European arena tour, but Clarke will not perform on stage. He will act as musical director remotely while keyboard technician Howard Rider plays the parts. When asked whether Tracy’s death is the main reason, Clarke answers simply: “Yes.”

Bell and Clarke describe their bond as closer to family than friendship. Their 40 years together have also made room for irreverence: their conversation turns from grief and the band’s future to jokes about clowns, old synths and Bell’s stagewear. The new record, Bell says, moves away from the synth sound of 2020’s The Neon towards piano and guitar.

content.headline: Cronos made Venom’s raw, theatrical metal a blueprint for black metal
content.shortHeadline: How Venom’s Cronos made metal raw and dangerous
content.standfirst: Conrad “Cronos” Lant turned punk’s unruly spirit into a faster, rougher form of heavy metal. Venom’s confrontational sound and stage persona helped inspire black metal and left a mark on thrash.

image.caption: Venom frontman Cronos pictured in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude

segments.body: When Venom emerged from Newcastle in the late 1970s, frontman and bassist Conrad “Cronos” Lant thought metal had grown “lame”. The band’s response was to bring punk’s do-it-yourself energy to heavier music: hoarse vocals, hammering riffs and lyrics that made occult imagery brash and confrontational.

segments.title: An influence with limits
segments.body: Venom’s 1982 album Black Metal gave a name to a subgenre that would take its own, sometimes violent, direction. Lant did not endorse that violence. “What a fucking shame that those guys are known for that and not for their music,” he told the Quietus, as the Norwegian scene became associated with church burnings and murder.

The band’s influence extended beyond black metal: the article traces its reach through the theatrical frontmen it inspired and the admiration of musicians including Anthrax’s Scott Ian and Megadeth’s Dave Mustaine. Lant later returned to Venom after a period away and remained committed to the abrasive sound that had made the group stand out.

content.headline: Heavensouls’ Cantu of the Sower turns sonic overload into a rush of beauty
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls makes breakneck chaos feel strangely serene
content.standfirst: On six tracks, Nigerian-American producer Chidi Obialo piles arcade glitter, distorted bass, brass and breakbeats into a vividly restless sound. The review finds a sense of wonder in the overload.

image.caption: Chidi Obialo, who records as Heavensouls.

sources.originalTitle: Add to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracks

segments.body: Heavensouls’ Cantu of the Sower thrives on abrupt shifts: arcade-like sparkle gives way to bass-heavy crunch, playful details to rushing brass. The review argues that the six-track release’s breakneck pace can become strangely calming, as if the music’s abundance tips from sensory overload into its own kind of release.

The record’s collages are not presented as randomness for its own sake. Found-sound snippets and a sample of civil rights activist Stokely Carmichael help ground the music in the artist’s attention to other people. Obialo, raised in Nigeria and based between Nigeria and Texas, has already released music in a wide range of styles; the review hears a distinctive gift for delirious, head-spinning beauty.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s My Aim Is True box set reveals how a songwriter took shape
content.shortHeadline: A 104-track set traces Elvis Costello before and after his debut
content.standfirst: The 49th-anniversary edition revisits a landmark debut with demos, live recordings and four companion discs. Its most valuable revelation is a gradual transformation rather than a bolt-from-the-blue arrival.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: My Aim Is True introduced Elvis Costello’s sharp, nervy songwriting in 1977. This five-CD edition gathers 104 tracks, including early recordings and live material, to trace how the songwriter developed before and around the album. The review finds the scale of the set can reopen the story rather than merely repeat a familiar classic-rock reissue formula.

segments.title: The work behind the breakthrough
segments.body: The early demos on The Blue Print suggest Costello was already a practiced songwriter, drawing on American roots music and writers including Randy Newman and Warren Zevon. The punk and new-wave edge associated with his debut emerged gradually, as his writing and public persona took shape.

The remaining discs document the shift towards the Attractions and a later reunion with members of the first album’s backing band. The review finds those recordings less essential, but sees the collection as a persuasive portrait of a young artist trying on influences and finding a voice.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul box set brings its shifting history into focus
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul is more than one album, this sprawling reissue argues
content.standfirst: The deluxe edition collects British and American track lists, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new remix. The review’s pleasure lies in hearing a pivotal album as a series of choices, not a single untouchable monument.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The new Rubber Soul set includes the UK and US editions, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a fresh remix. Its detailed recording history shows how quickly the Beatles made the album in 1965, under pressure to deliver it by Christmas, while still finding small, consequential touches in performance and arrangement.

segments.title: More than one version
segments.body: The US release removed some of the livelier tracks and replaced them with songs from Help!, making it a markedly different listening experience. The set also exposes the contrasts between mono and stereo mixes: one can make the record feel forceful and crowded, the other more spacious and precise.

Outtakes and studio fragments reveal paths the band considered and abandoned, bringing the canonical album back to human scale. The review’s conclusion is that no single edition can claim to be the definitive Rubber Soul: its many versions reflect the changing balance between artistic choices, technology and commerce.

content.headline: Stef Chura returns with a quieter, more ambivalent set of songs
content.shortHeadline: Stef Chura finds new shades of feeling on Dancing Alone on theConcrete
content.standfirst: After seven years away, the Detroit singer-songwriter favours understatement over the catharsis of her earlier work. The review hears familiar relationship anxieties made more compelling by her distinctive voice.

sources.originalTitle: Dancing Alone on the Concrete

segments.body: Dancing Alone on the Concrete is Stef Chura’s first album in seven years. Where her earlier songs often pushed towards loud catharsis, the review finds this record more restrained: its characters approach love and potential loss with an ambivalence that makes the feelings harder to resolve.

Chura’s voice remains the record’s most striking instrument, shifting with unusual ease between warmth and irritation. The arrangements are less consistently distinctive, but “Danny”—with contributions from R.E.M.’s Peter Buck and Mike Mills—offers a wistful, open-hearted hook, while the final song leaves uncertainty and hope suspended together.

content.headline: Lambchop’s Punching the Clown finds new clarity in a stripped-back sound
content.shortHeadline: Lambchop pares back the music, not Kurt Wagner’s storytelling
content.standfirst: Acoustic guitar, banjo and choir replace much of the band’s recent electronic texture. The review finds the simpler setting a compelling fit for Kurt Wagner’s funny, uneasy stories about ageing, loss and change.

sources.originalTitle: Punching the Clown

segments.body: Lambchop have repeatedly changed their sound over a 40-year career. Punching the Clown pares things back: Kurt Wagner sings with little studio effect, accompanied by acoustic guitar, banjo, sparse percussion and choral voices. The review hears an intimate, uncanny record rather than a straightforward return to an earlier style.

segments.title: Stories that refuse to settle
segments.body: Wagner’s lyrics move between the weighty and the absurd, slipping from family, death and politics into jokes or unexpected asides. The review singles out “The New World Wave”, a winding story that keeps its listener engaged even when its meaning remains unresolved.

The album’s reduced arrangements sharpen its sense of vulnerability. Songs such as “Weakened” dwell on illness and mortality, while “To Do” turns an ordinary task into a bleakly tender wish list. The review finds the record mysterious but unusually direct in its emotional effect.

content.headline: Digger divides critics: daring ecological farce or overblown misfire?
content.shortHeadline: Is Digger a bold Cruise experiment or an exhausting eco-satire?
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise plays an ageing oil tycoon at the centre of Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s climate satire. One review embraces its eccentric scale; two others find the performances, plotting or politics frustratingly shallow.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆
Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act

segments.body: Digger casts Cruise as an oil baron whose company’s drilling triggers a climate crisis. The film pairs a grotesque makeover and outsized performance with a story about corporate power and environmental disaster. Its approach has produced sharply different responses from critics.

perspectives.body: The BBC review calls the film a daring, politically blunt folly, arguing that its excess and Cruise’s commitment make it an exhilarating experiment—even if some scenes run too long.

segments.title: The case against
segments.body: The Guardian review sees a laborious, self-congratulatory satire whose big narrative turn undercuts its drama. The i review argues Cruise’s star persona overwhelms the character, making even a supposedly reflective moment feel like an actor consciously demonstrating his range.

perspectives.body: The i critic contends that Cruise’s highly self-conscious performance and fame make it difficult to see Digger as a character rather than a Tom Cruise showcase.

segments.body: The disagreement extends to what the film accomplishes with its environmental subject. The BBC finds its scenario newly plausible and its politics forceful; the Guardian considers the satire glib and notes that the film leaves a key argument about energy unchallenged. Viewers may find the film’s scale either its point or its problem.

content.headline: Paul Thomas Anderson captures Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert becomes a striking film
content.standfirst: Shot on 35mm, the 75-minute film keeps its attention on the Geese frontman, his piano and a rapt audience. The review praises an austere recording that preserves the unusual intimacy of a major concert.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.body: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall records a solo performance by the Geese frontman, filmed by Paul Thomas Anderson and a small team of camera operators. The film’s 35mm photography gives the hall a rich, tactile look, while its focus stays on Winter’s voice, piano and the audience listening.

Anderson largely avoids interviews, narration and other conventional documentary framing. The review finds that restraint preserves the silences and shifting light that made the concert feel intimate, though viewers who are not already drawn to Winter’s music may find little invitation beyond the performance itself.

content.headline: Brassed Off at 30: Mark Herman on the film’s enduring class politics
content.shortHeadline: Why Brassed Off still speaks to a new generation
content.standfirst: The writer-director expected his 1996 story of a Yorkshire colliery band to find a small audience. Three decades later, Mark Herman says its story of people facing economic upheaval still resonates—and worries similar films are harder to finance.

image.caption: Pete Postlethwaite in Brassed Off.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30-year anniversary

segments.body: Brassed Off follows the Grimley Colliery Band as its members face the closure of their pit and the loss of a way of life. Writer-director Mark Herman says the film’s mixture of comedy and politics helped audiences connect with it, despite his expectation that it might appeal only within a small radius of Barnsley.

segments.title: A story beyond its setting
segments.body: Herman believes the film’s longevity comes from its wider account of people being downtrodden. He says younger viewers still recognise its message, even though the story is rooted in the destruction of mining communities and the economic pressures of its time.

For the anniversary, Grimethorpe Colliery Band—the group that inspired the film—will perform its music alongside a screening at the Royal Albert Hall. Herman also says that films like Brassed Off would be difficult to get made today, as British cinema funding favours blockbusters and micro-budget projects over mid-budget work.

content.headline: Bassam Tariq turned a stalled Blade reboot into a personal thriller
content.shortHeadline: After Blade stalled, Bassam Tariq found freedom in a new thriller
content.standfirst: In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Mahershala Ali plays a devout father who works as a hitman. Director Bassam Tariq says the film grew from personal questions about faith and fatherhood—and from action work prepared for Marvel’s abandoned Blade project.

image.caption: Bassam Tariq at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.body: Mahershala Ali stars as Latif, a Houston father who is both devout and a contract killer, in Bassam Tariq’s thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Tariq frames the film’s violence through Latif’s religious code, while setting his struggle to raise three children against tensions between the city’s religious communities.

segments.title: From one project to another
segments.body: Tariq and Ali had worked together on the stalled Blade reboot, where they prepared action sequences before the project lost its script and stopped moving forward. Some of that fight work was reworked for the new film, which Tariq says gave him greater freedom to explore an intimate story outside the Marvel system.

The film’s opening search for breast milk draws on Tariq’s own experience after his first child was born and his wife was rushed to hospital. He says the crisis made him confront his anger at God and think about what his son needed from him as a father—a personal starting point for the thriller’s larger questions of grief, faith and responsibility.

content.headline: Why another Skywalker trilogy feels like a step backwards for Star Wars
content.shortHeadline: Star Wars should look beyond the Skywalker family
content.standfirst: Reports say Jon Watts may direct a new trilogy written by Simon Kinberg, with Daisy Ridley reportedly being considered to return as Rey. The films are not greenlit, and this commentary argues the saga has already brought the family story to a close twice.

image.caption: Daisy Ridley as Rey in The Rise of Skywalker.

sources.originalTitle: A new Skywalker trilogy for Star Wars? Going back to the same family-saga well is a waste of time

segments.body: A report says Lucasfilm has hired Jon Watts to direct the first film in a proposed new Skywalker trilogy written by Simon Kinberg, with Daisy Ridley reportedly eyed for a return as Rey. The films have not been greenlit, and details remain scarce.

The commentary questions whether the franchise can make another family saga feel necessary after the Skywalkers have repeatedly saved, lost and reclaimed the galaxy. It argues that some of the strongest recent Star Wars stories, including Rogue One and Andor, have found room beyond the family melodrama.

content.headline: Why horror keeps being pushed into the Golden Globes’ comedy category
content.shortHeadline: The Golden Globes leave horror with no comfortable category
content.standfirst: The Guardian argues that the Globes’ drama and musical-or-comedy split leaves films such as Obsession with an awkward awards choice. The debate reflects a wider problem for horror at ceremonies that shape early-season momentum.

image.caption: A still from Obsession.

sources.originalTitle: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies

segments.body: Focus Features will submit Obsession, a dark story of coercive love and violence, in the Golden Globes’ musical-or-comedy categories, according to the Hollywood Reporter. The article questions the fit: the film’s most obvious comic moment, it says, is a graphic killing rather than a conventional joke.

segments.title: A genre problem
segments.body: The Globes divide major categories between drama and musical or comedy, leaving horror without an obvious home. The article argues that horror can seem insufficiently “worthy” for drama while feeling like an uncomfortable match for comedy, even when the films succeed with critics and audiences.

The category choice can affect a film’s awards campaign because the Globes arrive early and help set momentum for the season. The article notes that a comedy-category placement helped The Substance’s Demi Moore win best actress, even as horror films continue to face an uphill path through major awards.

content.headline: James Dean beyond the rebel: the vulnerable actor behind the image
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean performance worth remembering is not the cool one
content.standfirst: A close look at Dean’s brief film career returns to the raw, vulnerable work behind his enduring image. The piece centres on East of Eden and the real emotion Elia Kazan drew from the young actor.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s screen career ended before it had properly begun: he died at 24, after three starring roles. His image as an emblem of youthful rebellion has lasted far beyond that small body of work, but this account argues that his most affecting moments reveal a more vulnerable performer.

segments.title: A scene that still cuts through
segments.body: During East of Eden, director Elia Kazan used Dean’s anger towards his father to reach the emotion of Cal, the rejected son he played. The essay returns to a scene in which Cal, hurt by his father’s refusal of a gift, breaks down and clings to him—an unscripted moment that complicates the familiar image of Dean as effortlessly cool.

The piece also traces how fame and an early death helped turn Dean into a myth, while distinguishing his restless, idiosyncratic performances from the comparisons with Marlon Brando that followed him. His vulnerability, rather than the poster-boy pose, is presented as the reason his acting still reaches viewers.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility’s new film finds Austen’s sisters still feel modern
content.shortHeadline: A new Sense and Sensibility asks how to balance feeling and reason
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation follows two sisters whose opposing approaches to love and security still feel familiar. Fiona Shaw, who plays Mrs Jennings, describes the film’s pared-back take on a character she recognises from her own upbringing.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility
Fiona Shaw: ‘They didn’t think women were funny when I was young’

segments.body: Georgia Oakley’s new film follows Elinor and Marianne Dashwood as they navigate love and financial insecurity after their family loses its fortune. The review sees their differing temperaments—one guarded, the other swept up in romance—as a modern tension between self-control and the pressure to live for passion.

segments.title: A different Mrs Jennings
segments.body: Fiona Shaw, who plays Mrs Jennings, says Oakley wanted a more pared-back version of the character than some adaptations have offered. Shaw sees her as someone who is benign but performs a role in a small community, where personalities can loom large.

perspectives.body: Shaw connects Mrs Jennings to people she knew growing up in Cork, and says she has reread Austen’s novel while preparing to discuss the adaptation.

segments.body: The film is darker and gloomier than the much-loved 1995 version, while retaining its period setting. The review argues that Austen’s question—whether to trust the head or the heart—still speaks to people trying to balance emotional openness with personal and financial uncertainty.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future raises questions about how it lost momentum
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who is off air. Can the BBC find a way back?
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special, leaving the show without a current Doctor. Fans and former contributors disagree about what went wrong, but remain hopeful it can return.

image.caption: Illustrations of Doctor Who actors including Peter Capaldi, Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its most recent series ended in 2025. The BBC has ended its co-production arrangement with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new funding partner. With no current Doctor announced, the show’s immediate future is unclear.

segments.title: What changed
segments.body: The article traces a history of reinvention, from the 2005 revival to the casting of Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa. It notes the online abuse that greeted both appointments, alongside criticism of scripts and a feeling among some viewers that recent episodes had grown too fantastical or no longer centred enough on the Doctor.

Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the series did not need a large Disney+ deal simply to tell good stories and wants the BBC to bring it back sooner. Former writer Nina Metivier points to the show’s themes of kindness and curiosity; other contributors see its capacity for change as a reason it can return.

perspectives.body: The sources do not settle on one cause for Doctor Who’s decline: the article presents concerns about financing, writing, casting and audience response, while fans stress the series’ long history of renewal.

content.headline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors slip-up gives the new series a thrilling start
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder is the show’s perfect opening
content.standfirst: Grant accidentally tells Joe Lycett he is a Traitor moments after being recruited, turning a high-stakes reveal into a comic crisis. The review argues that the cast’s unpredictability has given the celebrity edition fresh momentum.

image.caption: Richard E Grant and Maya Jama, the two initial Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: Richard E Grant’s first episode as a Traitor takes an unexpected turn when he tells Joe Lycett he has been recruited. The review describes the moment as an apparent blunder that throws his and fellow Traitor Maya Jama’s plans into disarray—and gives the series an unusually chaotic opening.

The cast’s star power is part of the appeal, but the review argues that celebrity expectations make the game more interesting: viewers arrive with ideas about how familiar figures might behave, then watch those assumptions unravel. The first episode’s other contestants are already showing signs of suspicion and misdirection.

A new twist requires the two Traitors to recruit a third player, with one of two candidates facing murder. The episode ends before that choice is revealed. For the reviewer, the combination of a near-sabotage and a cliffhanger makes this version feel more unpredictable rather than less.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson brings unapologetic pleasure to The Great British Bake Off
content.shortHeadline: Nigella’s Bake Off message: enjoy the cake, without guilt
content.standfirst: The new judge’s refusal to call food “naughty” becomes a welcome counter to calorie anxiety and body scrutiny. The essay sees her visible enjoyment as a meaningful change to the familiar baking-show ritual.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time

segments.body: On The Great British Bake Off, Nigella Lawson pushes back when fellow judge Paul Hollywood calls cookies “naughty”. “I don’t approve of talking about food as naughty,” she says. “We need to take our pleasures where we can in life.” The review sees the moment as a refreshing contrast to a culture that encourages women to monitor what they eat.

Lawson’s enthusiastic tasting is part of the point: she eats openly and treats pleasure as central to food, rather than turning every bake into a calculation of calories. The article contrasts that approach with the show’s previous judging style and argues that it offers viewers a brief respite from pressure to be thinner.

content.headline: War turns a celebrity divorce into glossy, high-stakes legal entertainment
content.shortHeadline: War is a shamelessly entertaining divorce drama
content.standfirst: Sienna Miller and Dominic West play a wealthy couple fighting over assets, reputation and legal tactics. The review celebrates the series’ plotting and performances as entertaining melodrama rather than a drama demanding emotional investment.

image.caption: James McArdle, Sienna Miller and Phoebe Fox in War.

sources.originalTitle: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

segments.body: War follows social-media mogul Morgan Henderson and actor Carla Duval as their public divorce draws in two rival law firms. Prenuptial agreements, money, press strategy and personal betrayals keep the dispute moving, while the lawyers’ own rivalries add another layer of mischief.

The review’s pleasure is in the show’s excess: old-fashioned offices, ambitious newcomers, scheming lawyers and an endless sequence of strategic reversals. It calls the series “high-quality balderdash”—a fast, glossy escape from the demands of daily news rather than a plea for sympathy for its rich characters.

The ensemble includes Miller and West, alongside Pip Torrens, Phoebe Fox, James McArdle, Celia Imrie and Archie Panjabi. The review praises the performances and George Kay’s control of the intricate plot, describing the result as soap opera with money, talent and plot to burn.

content.headline: Mike Flanagan’s Carrie brings Stephen King’s bullied teen into the present
content.shortHeadline: Carrie updates Stephen King’s horror for the social-media era
content.standfirst: The new series has drawn criticism for softening Carrie’s appearance and temperament, but a horror scholar sees its changes as a way to explore bullying now. The review praises the show while acknowledging its distance from the novel.

sources.originalTitle: Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part Carrie adapts Stephen King’s story of a bullied teenager whose telekinetic powers erupt under pressure. Some fans object that screen versions repeatedly cast conventionally attractive actors and depict Carrie as more naïve and sympathetic than the angry, “plain” character in the book.

segments.title: Adaptation and change
segments.body: This version moves Carrie into the present and makes her a newcomer to school after being homeschooled. Horror scholar Sorcha Ní Fhlainn argues that its focus on social media updates familiar forms of teenage bullying, even as Carrie’s home-sewn clothes and isolation mark her as an outsider.

perspectives.body: Ní Fhlainn sees the new series as working on its own terms, while film-maker Liam Gavin notes that casting and production funding can also shape adaptation choices.

segments.body: The BBC review ultimately calls the series engrossing and surprising, with strong performances, while recognising that the novel’s more forceful, self-aware Carrie remains a point of comparison. The debate is not only about fidelity but about whose bodies and personalities screen adaptations are willing to portray.

content.headline: Lenny Rush makes The Reluctant Vampire a comedy about belonging
content.shortHeadline: Lenny Rush finds a place for the awkward vampire
content.standfirst: The 17-year-old actor leads a sitcom adapted from an Eric Morecambe children’s book, playing a boy who discovers he is not a vampire at all. Rush sees the character’s struggle to fit in as a familiar teenage story.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: In The Reluctant Vampire, Lenny Rush plays Val, a young member of a vampire household whose teeth are not sharp and who dislikes blood. The comic twist is that he is not a vampire at all, but a human—an outsider in a family and world that expect him to belong.

segments.title: Comedy with a wider audience
segments.body: The series adapts a children’s book written by Eric Morecambe in the 1980s, with scripts by Neil and Rob Gibbons, the team behind Alan Partridge. Rush says the show should work for adults as well as children, mixing broad comic situations with genuine pathos.

Rush says messages from parents have shown him that his visibility has helped some disabled children feel more confident. He does not describe acting as an inspirational mission, but sees Val’s story of trying and failing to fit in as something that can resonate well beyond the show’s supernatural setting.

content.headline: Sharon Horgan’s Youth exposes a familiar problem for women on TV
content.shortHeadline: Youth’s “everywoman” is still expected to look extraordinary
content.standfirst: The review praises Horgan’s writing but questions her casting as a middle-aged woman under pressure, arguing that television still expects female leads to be exceptionally beautiful even when their stories claim everyday realism.

image.caption: Sharon Horgan in Youth.

sources.originalTitle: Sharon Horgan’s Youth has one big problem

segments.body: Sharon Horgan created, wrote and stars in Youth as Alex, a 50-something literary agent juggling a troubled teenager, ageing parents and a difficult career. The review calls the character an “everywoman”, then questions whether Horgan’s glamorous screen presence makes that identification harder for viewers.

segments.title: A persistent double standard
segments.body: The essay argues that women on television are still expected to meet stricter beauty standards than men. It notes Horgan’s own comments about the treatments she uses to look like “a human woman on TV” and asks why a relatable woman’s appearance so often has to be explained or exceptional.

The criticism is directed at a wider industry convention, not Horgan’s talent. The article credits her for creating complex roles for women, while suggesting that more performers with ordinary, varied appearances should be allowed to lead stories without their looks becoming a tragic plot point.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights at 20: the football drama that found a life beyond sport
content.shortHeadline: Friday Night Lights made small-town Texas feel real
content.standfirst: Peter Berg’s drama used a book about high-school football in Odessa as a starting point for a story about community, race and pressure. Its naturalistic performances and sense of place helped it endure despite ratings struggles.

image.caption: Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: First broadcast in 2006, Friday Night Lights turned H.G. “Buzz” Bissinger’s account of high-school football in Odessa into a fictional story set in Dillon, Texas. The series explored the expectations placed on young players and the town around them, including the racial divisions and pressures documented in the book.

segments.title: A different kind of network drama
segments.body: Director Peter Berg encouraged improvisation, used handheld cameras and let actors adapt dialogue once key story beats were met. The article argues that this approach gave the show an unusually naturalistic feel, while its women characters were given lives beyond the football field.

The series faced low ratings, a shortened second season and a move to a cable co-production, but ran for five seasons and 76 episodes. Its legacy includes early roles for Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan, alongside the work of Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton as the Taylor family.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has superb combat but too little else to sustain it
content.shortHeadline: E-Day’s combat soars; its repetitive campaign does not
content.standfirst: The prequel makes the series’ cover-based shooting feel better than ever, but repeated routes, collectibles and weak exploration drain the momentum. The review finds a strong action game buried in a safe, repetitive campaign.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: Gears of War: E-Day returns to the alien invasion that shaped the series, following Marcus Fenix and a squad of soldiers as creatures erupt from the ground. The review finds the combat excellent: movement is more fluid, weapons feel weighty and damaged environments respond vividly to firefights.

segments.title: A campaign that circles back
segments.body: The game repeatedly sends players across the same devastated city, sometimes crossing the same bridge several times. Large areas are crowded with collectibles and side objectives, while wandering away from the main path can trigger a mission failure—even as the game encourages exploration.

The review argues that E-Day is most effective when it leans into enclosed, horror-tinged encounters, but says those moments make up too little of the campaign. The series’ tactical, cover-based shooting remains a strength; the levels and supporting systems do not build on it enough.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil film recreates the unease of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: This Resident Evil film adapts the feeling of playing
content.standfirst: Rather than centre familiar heroes, the film follows an ordinary courier through an outbreak, scarce ammunition and a succession of game-like locations. The argument is that it adapts the series’ mechanics and mood, not just its lore.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger with actor Austin Abrams on the Resident Evil set.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil film does not centre familiar characters such as Leon, Claire or Ada Wong. Instead, it follows courier Bryan Hodukavich as a virus outbreak traps him in a world he barely understands, where he finds weapons but never enough ammunition.

segments.title: A player’s point of view
segments.body: The film moves through settings familiar from the games—a farmhouse, a road tunnel, a hospital and a sewer—and uses recordings and brief encounters to reveal the story. The article argues that this structure evokes the experience of exploring a game world, where danger and information arrive in fragments.

perspectives.body: The writer sees the film as an unusually faithful adaptation because it recreates the vulnerability and uncertainty of play, rather than relying on familiar heroes and plot points.

segments.body: The piece places Cregger’s approach alongside films that examine video-game mechanics directly. It also draws on Resident Evil creator Shinji Mikami’s view that horror is strongest when players are unsure whether their character will survive—a condition Bryan inhabits throughout.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers the exhilaration of a great aerial dogfight
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes its Top Gun fantasy fly
content.standfirst: The new entry pairs spectacular skies and thrilling combat with a more involving story than the series usually offers. The review finds its missions varied and moving, while noting cluttered objectives and unavailable multiplayer during testing.

image.caption: A fighter aircraft in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 casts players as a fictional ace pilot whose legend begins as wartime propaganda. Its dogfights deliver the series’ familiar rush of weaving through missiles and firing on enemy planes, now backed by striking clouds, cinematic camera work and a story the reviewer found unexpectedly affecting.

segments.title: Learning to fly
segments.body: Newcomers can choose simplified controls and training scenarios, while experienced players can opt for a more demanding scheme with advanced manoeuvres. Missions vary from bombing and escort work to tracking stealth aircraft and attacking a railgun-equipped land battleship.

The review’s reservations are mainly about readability: visual clutter can obscure objectives, and the clouds can be disorienting even as they look impressive. The online multiplayer mode was available only briefly during the review period, so the reviewer could not assess it.

content.headline: Roblox scams are tricking children into handing over accounts and Robux
content.shortHeadline: How fake Roblox login pages steal children’s Robux
content.standfirst: Fraudsters lure players with promises of free currency, then use imitation login pages to collect passwords and personal data. Security experts advise families to open Roblox directly and never share authentication codes.

image.caption: Roblox advises users to access the service directly and avoid links from unknown senders.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Children are being targeted by scams promising free Robux, Roblox’s in-game currency. Links shared in YouTube and TikTok comments or on Discord can lead to imitation login pages that look legitimate; after entering their details, a child may be redirected to the real site with little indication anything is wrong.

segments.title: Protecting an account
segments.body: NordVPN researchers say they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages over seven days. Its experts advise children to open Roblox through the official app or website, avoid unfamiliar links and treat two-factor authentication and backup codes like passwords.

Roblox says it has security measures including two-factor authentication, but warns it cannot guarantee that compromised accounts or lost virtual items will be restored. In very limited circumstances it may recover items or their value; families should not assume stolen Robux will be returned.

content.headline: Playing Call of Duty with my son brought back the joy of gaming
content.shortHeadline: A father and son revisit the game that started their bond
content.standfirst: Seventeen years after playing Modern Warfare 2 together when his son was five, a father returns to its co-op missions with him as an adult. The reunion becomes a story about teamwork, memory and a limited time together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the co-op game father and son revisit.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: A father and his 22-year-old son revisit the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 co-op missions they first attempted in 2009, when the boy was five. This time they finish levels they once could not, learning to combine the father’s cautious sniping with his son’s more impulsive style.

Their old shorthand for the missions—“the guard dogs in the snow”, “defend the garage from five waves of attack”—turns repeated failures into a shared joke. Over time, the two players find a rhythm and celebrate completing challenges that had defeated them as a child and an adult.

The piece becomes a reflection on how gaming changes with age and responsibility.
