The father knows their time living together is temporary, but his son says he will remember these sessions as some of their best times. The closing emotion is less about nostalgia than the pleasure of being present together.

content.headline: The Pokémon volunteers who keep competitive play running
content.shortHeadline: Meet the volunteer judges behind Pokémon tournaments
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, Pokémon Professors refereed matches, helped new competitors and kept events safe. Their work can also mean handling tense rulings and upset players, often out of public view.

image.caption: Attendees at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: Pokémon Professors are volunteers who help run official competitions, from teaching players to judging matches and managing event logistics. Around 300 were present at the 2026 world championships in San Francisco, according to a Pokémon Company International representative.

segments.title: More than enforcing rules
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard describes checking match results, ensuring the venue is safe and making decisions when disputes arise. Evelyne de Groot, who travelled from the Netherlands, says a professor also needs to give players clear instructions and help them enjoy the event.

The work can involve difficult calls and angry competitors. Byard says players may see only part of a situation, while judges must make decisions based on the full account. The article also notes that volunteers’ compensation varies and that the Pokémon Company International declined to give an official explanation of its arrangements.

perspectives.body: Byard’s account of the pressure of making contested rulings sits alongside de Groot’s emphasis on welcoming new players and building a positive community.

content.headline: Why gamers are pushing back against Wolverine’s constant guidance
content.shortHeadline: Players want games to leave room for discovery
content.standfirst: Viral clips of Marvel’s Wolverine highlight a wider frustration with games that mark every route, target and task. The argument is that good design needs friction: enough uncertainty for players to exercise judgment and feel achievement.

image.caption: Marvel’s Wolverine, criticised for its frequent gameplay cues.

sources.originalTitle: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay

segments.body: Marvel’s Wolverine has drawn online ridicule for visual cues that steer players towards objectives, targets and collectibles. The article treats the game as a conspicuous example of a broader design habit: blockbuster games increasingly explain what to do before players have a chance to work it out.

segments.title: Difficulty versus friction
segments.body: The writer distinguishes a game’s difficulty from its friction—the intentional distance between a player and a goal. Clear instructions can prevent players getting stuck, but too much guidance removes the agency and learning that make overcoming a challenge satisfying.

Examples such as Hollow Knight: Silksong and Blue Prince illustrate different forms of high friction, while straightforward combat games can be low-friction but difficult. The article hopes the reaction to Wolverine will remind developers and executives that players can be trusted to explore and learn.

content.headline: GTA VI’s virtual romance debate reflects real relationship anxieties
content.shortHeadline: Is GTA VI romance cheating—or a sign of disconnection?
content.standfirst: Social-media users argue that maintaining the game’s relationship between Lucia and Jason could cross a line. The article rejects a universal definition of cheating but takes seriously the insecurity behind some players’ concerns.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: A discussion about Grand Theft Auto VI has focused less on its violence than its protagonists’ romance. Players will be able to strengthen Lucia and Jason’s bond through dates, messages and other interactions. Some social-media users say that taking part in these scenes amounts to cheating on a real partner.

segments.title: Different boundaries
segments.body: The article argues that a fictional romance should not automatically be treated as infidelity, while recognising that individual couples may set different boundaries. It also distinguishes game relationships from AI companionship services, which raise a different set of questions.

Behind the online jokes, the writer sees a concern about partners investing care and attention in fictional relationships while neglecting real ones. The debate, the article suggests, reflects wider loneliness and dissatisfaction rather than a problem that a game alone can resolve.

perspectives.body: Sex educator Dee Whitnell argues that feeling underappreciated in a relationship can make a partner’s investment in a virtual character genuinely frustrating, even if others consider the comparison absurd.
